High Blood Lead Result for a Child: What Happens at Home

A high blood lead result sends parents straight to the question of where it came from. In an older Cleveland house the home itself is one of the first places to check, because deteriorating lead paint and the dust it makes are common sources.

Call {{PHONE_DISPLAY}}

Request a call

Describe what you are seeing in the house and we will follow up. Prefer to talk? Call {{PHONE_DISPLAY}}.

For service inquiries only. If someone is in immediate danger or you suspect acute poisoning, call 911 or Poison Help at 1-800-222-1222.

Start with the child's health care provider

CDC says a blood lead test is the best way to find out if a child has lead poisoning, and a child with lead poisoning may not show any signs. CDC uses a blood lead reference value of 3.5 micrograms per deciliter to identify children with higher levels than most, as explained on its reference value page. Your provider decides on follow-up testing and care, and this site does not give medical advice.

Then look at the home

EPA notes that the most common home-based source of lead exposure is deteriorating lead-based paint and the resulting dust. In a home built before 1978, a lead risk assessment checks paint condition, dust and soil to find the likely sources. If you only need to know where lead paint is, an inspection does that.

Habits that reduce dust while you wait

Keep painted surfaces in good condition, wet-wipe window sills and floors rather than dry dusting, and keep children from chewing on sills and rails. EPA lists these steps for making a home lead-safe. Do not scrape or sand paint yourself while you wait for a plan.

Fixing the source

The assessment will recommend controls, from encapsulation to window replacement to abatement, followed by clearance testing so you know the dust is down.

Common questions

Does lead exposure always cause symptoms?

No. CDC says most children with any lead in their blood have no obvious immediate symptoms, which is why testing matters.

Can I just move out of the house?

That is a family decision to make with your provider and the local health department. The home still needs to be assessed if other children or future occupants will live there.

How to Tell If Your Paint Is Lead Paint

People search for this when they notice paint flaking off an old window or porch rail and wonder whether it is dangerous. The honest answer is that you cannot tell by looking, but the age of the house and the condition of the paint tell you how seriously to take it.

Call {{PHONE_DISPLAY}}

Request a call

Describe what you are seeing in the house and we will follow up. Prefer to talk? Call {{PHONE_DISPLAY}}.

For service inquiries only. If someone is in immediate danger or you suspect acute poisoning, call 911 or Poison Help at 1-800-222-1222.

Start with the age of the house

Lead was banned in residential paint in 1978. EPA says that 87 percent of homes built before 1940 have some lead-based paint, and 24 percent of homes built between 1960 and 1978 do. The City of Cleveland graphic on its lead page notes that about 80 percent of homes in the city were built before 1980, so for a house in Cleveland the age question usually points toward testing. You can find the year built on the county property record.

Signs that deserve attention

Look at paint that is peeling, chipping, chalking or cracking. Look hard at the parts of the house that rub or take impact: window sashes and sills, door frames, stair treads and railings, and porch floors and posts. The EPA family booklet names these same areas. Fine, powdery residue on a window sill is also worth taking seriously, because that is how lead dust shows up in practice.

Lead paint is not always visible damage. Intact lead paint under newer layers can be fine until someone sands, scrapes or heats it during a remodel.

What not to do

Do not dry scrape, sand or burn the paint to find out what is under it. That is the fastest way to turn a stable surface into a dust problem. EPA's advice in the booklet is to keep painted surfaces in good condition, get your home checked by a certified risk assessor, and not to try removing lead-based paint yourself.

How you find out for sure

Confirming lead paint takes testing. A lead paint inspection says which surfaces contain lead, and a risk assessment says which of those are hazards. If you are comparing options, the guide on testing, abatement or renovation helps you pick.

On symptoms: CDC notes that a child with lead poisoning may not have visible signs or symptoms, so a blood test is how exposure gets found. See what to do after a high blood lead result.

Common questions

Can I use a home test kit?

A kit only checks the spot you swab. A full inspection or assessment covers the whole home and is done by licensed people, which matters if you plan to rent, sell or repair based on the result.

My house was built in 1985. Do I need to worry?

The ban on residential lead paint took effect in 1978, and the City of Cleveland says houses built after 1978 are exempt from its lead safe certificate law. Older layers or old components added later are the exceptions to ask about.

Remodeling an Older Cleveland House Without Spreading Lead

Cleveland rehabs often start with demolition: tearing out trim, cutting into plaster, stripping a porch. In a house built before 1978 each of those jobs can release lead dust, which is why the federal renovation rule exists and why testing before a remodel saves you from surprises halfway through the job.

Call {{PHONE_DISPLAY}}

Request a call

Describe what you are seeing in the house and we will follow up. Prefer to talk? Call {{PHONE_DISPLAY}}.

For service inquiries only. If someone is in immediate danger or you suspect acute poisoning, call 911 or Poison Help at 1-800-222-1222.

What the renovation rule requires

EPA states that anyone paid to perform work that disturbs painted surfaces in homes, childcare facilities and preschools built before 1978 must be certified, and their workers trained in lead-safe work practices. That covers most home contracting, including window replacement, trim removal and demolition that touches painted surfaces.

Renovation is not abatement

The two are easy to confuse. EPA explains that renovation disturbs paint as a consequence of the work, while abatement is done to address lead. A contractor with renovation certification is not automatically allowed to do abatement, and a lead hazard control order needs licensed abatement professionals in Ohio.

Test before the demo starts

If you know which surfaces contain lead, you can plan around them: replace a lead window instead of sanding it, seal a wall instead of cutting it open, or schedule containment where it matters. Start with testing and inspection, and consider lead-safe window replacement for the windows.

Finish with cleanup that you can verify

Dust left behind is the real risk to the people living in the house afterward. Clearance testing and cleanup is how you confirm it.

Common questions

Does this apply to my own home?

The rule applies to paid work. If you hire a contractor for a pre-1978 home, ask whether they hold EPA lead-safe renovation certification.

Is lead-safe renovation the same as abatement?

No. See testing, abatement or renovation for how the two differ.

Lead Testing, Abatement or Renovation: Which Service Do You Need?

Callers rarely start with the right service name. They say there is paint peeling on a porch, a landlord notice, a kid who tested high, or a kitchen they want to gut. This guide sorts those situations into the service that actually fits.

Call {{PHONE_DISPLAY}}

Request a call

Describe what you are seeing in the house and we will follow up. Prefer to talk? Call {{PHONE_DISPLAY}}.

For service inquiries only. If someone is in immediate danger or you suspect acute poisoning, call 911 or Poison Help at 1-800-222-1222.

You are not sure there is lead at all

If the house was built in 1978 or earlier and you do not know what is in the paint, start with testing and inspection. It tells you which surfaces contain lead without committing you to any work.

Someone may already be getting exposed

A child with a high blood test, a pregnant household member, or visible dust and chips around a window point toward a risk assessment, which looks at hazards, and often dust and soil testing. The page on a high blood lead result covers the first steps at home.

You need to fix a known hazard

When an assessment or an order calls for lead hazard control, that is abatement: removal, replacement, or encapsulation and enclosure. EPA separates abatement from renovation work by purpose: abatement exists to address lead, while renovation disturbs paint as a side effect.

You are remodeling and lead is a side issue

A kitchen, bath or porch project in a pre-1978 home is renovation. Paid renovation work in those homes falls under EPA's renovation, repair and painting rule, which requires certified firms and lead-safe work practices. See renovating a pre-1978 Cleveland house.

You own a Cleveland rental

The city requires a certificate or exemption for pre-1978 rentals, and the process begins with an assessment. The page on lead safe certificates has the steps.

Common questions

What is the difference between abatement and renovation?

Abatement is work done to permanently eliminate lead paint hazards. Renovation is any other work that happens to disturb paint, and it still needs lead-safe practices in older homes.

Do I need clearance testing after every job?

Clearance examinations follow abatement. Renovation has its own cleaning verification steps. See clearance testing and cleanup.

Lead Abatement in Cleveland, OH

About 80 percent of Cleveland homes were built before 1980, which means toxic lead paint is a fair assumption in much of the city until a test says otherwise. Whether you found peeling paint on a porch, received a rental notice or plan to remodel, start by describing what you see and we will point you to the right lead service.

What toxic lead abatement actually covers

Most people searching for lead abatement are really trying to answer a smaller question first: does my house have a lead problem, and what kind? The word covers a chain of separate services. A lead paint inspection finds lead paint. A risk assessment finds hazards. Abatement itself, meaning lead paint removal, replacement, enclosure or encapsulation, is the permanent fix, and clearance testing confirms the dust is gone afterward.

Cleveland adds a local layer. The city's own Lead Safe Program says rental properties built before 1978 must obtain a lead safe certification or an exemption, and the city presumes those rentals contain lead-based paint. Owner-occupied homes are not required to certify, but they face the same paint, the same dust and the same remodeling risks.

Ohio also controls who may do this work. State rules require a license for lead inspections, risk assessments and clearance exams, so one of the first questions to ask anyone is for their license.

Cleveland Lead Safe Certificate for Rental Property Owners

If you rent out a Cleveland property built before 1978, the city requires a lead safe certificate or an exemption. The process runs through the city portal, starts with a licensed lead risk assessment, and often turns up lead work to handle before the paperwork is finished.

Request a call

For service inquiries only. If someone is in immediate danger or you suspect acute poisoning, call 911 or Poison Help at 1-800-222-1222.

Which properties are covered

The City of Cleveland's Lead Safe Program page says rental properties built before 1978 must obtain a Lead Safe Certification or an exemption, and that owner-occupied properties do not need to be certified. The requirement comes from legislation passed in 2019, and under the codified ordinance any rental built before January 1, 1978 is presumed to contain lead-based paint.

The city also notes that houses built after 1978 are exempt, so the year built is the first thing to confirm.

The steps in order

The city's step-by-step submission guide lists what you need: the rental registration number, the parcel number and year built, which you can look up on the Cuyahoga County property site, and email addresses for the owner and the risk assessor. The city FAQ adds that once you have a lead risk assessment you can apply for the certificate or a 20-year exemption through the city's Accela portal.

The risk assessment itself is described on the page about lead risk assessment. If the report finds hazards, plan for abatement, encapsulation or window replacement before you finalize.

Where lead work fits in

A certificate is paperwork, but the point of the program is safer housing. Rental units are where deteriorated paint tends to go unreported, because tenants are not the ones deciding on repairs. Fixing the hazard first, then confirming with clearance testing where required, is the sturdier path.

Rules and forms change. Check the city pages linked above for the current process before you submit.

Common questions

Does my owner-occupied house need a certificate?

No, the city says owner-occupied properties do not need to be certified. A risk assessment can still make sense if you are buying, renovating or have young children at home.

Who performs the lead risk assessment?

A licensed lead risk assessor. Ohio requires that license for risk assessments under rule 3701-32-03.

What is the 20-year exemption?

The city's FAQ says owners can apply for a certificate or a 20-year exemption after getting an assessment. The city's guide explains who qualifies, so read it before you apply.

Lead Clearance Testing and Cleanup After the Work Is Done

After anything that disturbs old paint, the dust left behind is what harms children, and it is invisible. Clearance testing is the lab-backed check that a room is clean, not merely swept, and it is the finish line for a Cleveland abatement or lead-safe renovation.

Call {{PHONE_DISPLAY}}

Request a call

Describe what you are seeing in the house and we will follow up. Prefer to talk? Call {{PHONE_DISPLAY}}.

For service inquiries only. If someone is in immediate danger or you suspect acute poisoning, call 911 or Poison Help at 1-800-222-1222.

Why sweeping and mopping are not enough

Lead dust is fine enough to sit in the grain of wood floors, in window troughs and in the corners of sills. Regular brooms and household vacuums can lift it into the air. Lead-safe cleanup uses HEPA vacuums and wet wiping in a set order, which is also what the EPA renovation rule expects of certified firms.

Cleanup is also why people end up needing dust wipe testing: you cannot judge the result by looking.

What a clearance exam is

A clearance exam is a visual inspection plus dust wipe samples sent to an accredited lab. It follows lead abatement, and in Ohio the exam must be done by a licensed lead inspector or lead risk assessor, as laid out in the state rule.

EPA lowered the post-abatement dust-lead levels in October 2024, as described on the EPA hazard standards page, and lab results are compared with those levels.

If a room does not pass

A failed sample is not unusual and it is not a catastrophe. The usual response is to clean the area again and retest. Ask the person doing the exam how failures are handled before the job starts.

For the work that comes before clearance, see lead paint removal and abatement and lead-safe window replacement.

Common questions

Is clearance testing required after every renovation?

Not every job. It follows abatement, and a verification step applies to certified renovation work. Ask your provider which one applies to your project.

Can I use a regular shop vacuum for cleanup?

A standard vacuum can blow fine dust back into the room. Lead-safe cleanup calls for HEPA filtration.

Who does the testing?

A licensed lead inspector or lead risk assessor, as Ohio requires for clearance examinations.

How lead dust testing works

A dust wipe test uses a pre-moistened wipe on a measured square of surface, such as a floor, a window sill or the trough where a window sash sits. The wipe goes to an accredited lab, and the lab reports how much lead was collected. EPA's dust-lead hazard standards now treat any reportable level as a hazard in pre-1978 homes, so a lab result is the number that matters.

Windows are the usual hot spot. When a painted sash slides against a painted frame, it grinds a little paint into fine dust each time, and that dust lands on the sill and the floor below.

Soil around the house

Exterior paint on siding, porches and trim sheds slowly with weather and repainting. Soil near the foundation, under porches and along drip lines can end up holding that paint. Soil sampling is worth considering where children play, where pets dig, or where you plan a vegetable bed.

This service covers lead from paint and dust. Drinking water is a separate question handled through your water supplier and plumbing, not through paint testing.

Where testing fits in the bigger picture

Dust and soil samples are usually part of a full risk assessment. They are also how a clearance exam confirms that a room is clean after work, which is covered under clearance testing and cleanup. If you only know that paint is peeling and want to understand what it might mean, start with the guide on telling whether paint is lead paint.

Common questions

Should I test the soil in my garden?

If the house is older than 1978 and has exterior paint that has flaked, it is reasonable to ask for soil sampling before planting food crops or setting up a play area near the foundation.

Can I clean lead dust up myself?

Ordinary sweeping and dry dusting can spread fine dust. EPA steps for making a home lead-safe cover safer cleaning habits, and a risk assessment tells you whether more is needed.

Is a dust test the same as a paint inspection?

No. An inspection checks paint. A dust test checks what has already come off the paint. The two answer different questions, which is why they are often combined.

Lead Paint Encapsulation and Enclosure: Sealing Instead of Stripping

Sometimes the safest way to deal with lead paint is to leave it in place and lock it away. Encapsulation seals it behind a bonded coating, and enclosure covers it with a rigid barrier, which can suit the plaster walls and wood trim found throughout older Cleveland houses.

For service inquiries only. If someone is in immediate danger or you suspect acute poisoning, call 911 or Poison Help at 1-800-222-1222.

How the two methods differ

Encapsulation, as HUD describes it, makes lead-based paint inaccessible by forming a barrier from a liquid-applied coating or an adhesively bonded covering. Enclosure uses a rigid, durable material fastened over the surface. Both count as abatement methods when done to permanently control a hazard, which is different from ordinary repainting.

Painting over lead paint with regular paint is maintenance. It can help keep a stable surface in good shape, but it is not a substitute for a plan based on an assessment.

Where sealing makes sense

Good candidates are surfaces in sound condition that nobody rubs, bumps or chews: interior walls, ceilings and some trim. Poor candidates are the parts that move or take impact, such as window sashes, door edges, stair treads and porch railings. For those, replacement or removal usually works better.

Sealed surfaces also need to be watched. The same HUD guidance points out that removal gives a long-term fix needing little follow-up, while encapsulation depends on the barrier staying intact, so ask your assessor how and when to re-check it.

Questions to ask before you choose

Ask which surfaces the plan covers and why each method was picked for each one. Ask how the barrier will be inspected later, and ask what will be tested after the work. A clearance exam, covered on the page about clearance testing, is the check that dust levels are acceptable afterward.

Common questions

Is encapsulation permanent?

It is intended as a long-term control, but it relies on the barrier staying bonded and undamaged, so it needs periodic checks.

Can I use lead encapsulant paint from a store?

Product choice and application matter for whether the work counts as abatement. Ask a licensed assessor or abatement contractor before you buy anything.

What about windows?

Windows are friction surfaces and rarely good candidates for sealing. See the page on lead-safe window replacement.

Lead Paint Testing and Inspection in Cleveland, OH

Most Cleveland housing was built long before lead paint was banned in 1978, and paint that looks sound can still contain lead. An inspection tests the painted surfaces in a home one by one, so you know where the lead is before a sale, a repaint or a rehab starts.

Request a call

Describe what you are seeing in the house and we will follow up. Prefer to talk? Call {{PHONE_DISPLAY}}.

For service inquiries only. If someone is in immediate danger or you suspect acute poisoning, call 911 or Poison Help at 1-800-222-1222.

What a lead paint inspection tells you

A lead paint inspection answers one question: which painted or coated surfaces in this home contain lead-based paint. The inspector checks surfaces such as window sashes, door casings, trim, stair parts and porch components, usually with an instrument that reads the paint in place or with paint samples sent to a lab. The EPA explains the difference between inspections, risk assessments and abatements in plain language, and the short version is that an inspection finds lead paint but does not by itself say whether it is a hazard today.

That distinction matters in an old house. Intact lead paint on a wall that nobody touches is a different situation from the same paint on a window that slides open and shut every day. If you need to know about hazards, the next step is a lead risk assessment.

When people order testing

The usual triggers are buying an older home, preparing a rental, planning a remodel that will touch paint, or noticing paint that is chipping, chalking or peeling. Parents of young children often ask for it after a pediatrician mentions lead. Landlords ask because the City of Cleveland presumes that any rental built before January 1, 1978 has lead-based paint, as stated in the city ordinance.

A single swab on a single door only tells you about that door. A full inspection covers the whole home, which is why the results are useful for planning work and for deciding between encapsulation and removal.

Who is allowed to do it in Ohio

Ohio law does not let just anyone run these tests for hire. Under rule 3701-32-03 of the Ohio Administrative Code, a lead inspection requires a valid lead inspector or lead risk assessor license. When you call, ask who will do the testing and ask to see the license before you schedule anything.

If you are weighing testing against a bigger decision, the guide on testing, abatement or renovation walks through which service fits which situation.

Common questions

How do I know if my paint is lead paint?

You cannot tell by looking. Age is the first clue, since EPA reports that 87 percent of homes built before 1940 have some lead-based paint, and testing is the only way to confirm it on a specific surface.

Do I need lead testing if my house was built after 1978?

The City of Cleveland states that houses built after 1978 are exempt from its lead safe certificate law, so testing is mainly a question for homes built in 1978 or earlier.

What should I do with the results?

A positive result means the next call is about hazards and a plan, not panic. Keep painted surfaces in good condition, avoid dry scraping or sanding, and talk through a risk assessment and the right fix for each surface.

Lead Paint Removal and Abatement in Cleveland, OH

Abatement is the permanent fix for lead paint hazards: removing the paint, replacing the part that carries it, or sealing it in for good, under containment. In older Cleveland housing the usual targets are window sashes, door frames, porch parts and stair rails, where painted surfaces wear against each other.

Call {{PHONE_DISPLAY}}

Request a call

Describe what you are seeing in the house and we will follow up. Prefer to talk? Call {{PHONE_DISPLAY}}.

For service inquiries only. If someone is in immediate danger or you suspect acute poisoning, call 911 or Poison Help at 1-800-222-1222.

What abatement means

Abatement is a defined term, not a synonym for repainting. HUD's abatement guidance describes it as removing the building component or the paint, or permanently enclosing lead-based paint hazards. The four recognized approaches are removal, replacement, enclosure and encapsulation, and a good assessor picks a different one for different surfaces in the same house.

Removal takes the paint off the surface. Replacement takes out the whole component, such as a window or door. Enclosure covers the paint with a rigid, durable barrier, and encapsulation seals it with a coating or bonded covering. Those last two are covered on the page about encapsulation and enclosure.

Why it is not a weekend project

EPA tells homeowners not to try to remove lead-based paint themselves. Dry scraping, sanding and heat guns turn paint into fine dust and fumes, and that is how a stable surface becomes a hazard. Abatement work is done with containment, protective gear, controlled cleanup and a final check.

Ohio also regulates who does the work. The Ohio Department of Health's abatement FAQ says a licensed lead abatement contractor or project designer is required in situations such as working on a property under a lead hazard control order, so ask about licensing up front.

After the work: clearance

Abatement is not finished when the crew leaves. A clearance examination checks that dust left behind is below the standard, and in Ohio that exam must be performed by a licensed lead inspector or risk assessor. You can read more on clearance testing and cleanup.

If your project is a remodel rather than a lead hazard fix, the rules are different. The page on renovating a pre-1978 Cleveland house explains the renovation rule and how it differs from abatement.

Common questions

Is lead abatement the same as lead remediation?

People use the words loosely, but abatement has a specific meaning: measures intended to permanently eliminate lead paint hazards. EPA draws the line between abatement and renovation work based on the reason for the work.

Do I have to remove all the lead paint in my house?

Not necessarily. A risk assessment points to the hazards, and some surfaces can be handled by enclosure or encapsulation instead of removal.

Can I scrape lead paint myself to save a step?

EPA advises against it. Disturbing the paint is what creates the dust, so the work is better left to trained, licensed people.

Lead Risk Assessment for Cleveland Homes and Rentals

A risk assessment looks at the hazards, not just the paint: chipping surfaces, dust on floors and window sills, and bare soil near the house. In Cleveland it is also the starting point for rental owners applying for a lead safe certificate, and the step families take when a child has had a high blood lead test.

Request a call

Describe what you are seeing in the house and we will follow up. Prefer to talk? Call {{PHONE_DISPLAY}}.

For service inquiries only. If someone is in immediate danger or you suspect acute poisoning, call 911 or Poison Help at 1-800-222-1222.

Inspection versus risk assessment

People mix these up constantly. An inspection says where lead paint is. A risk assessment says where it is hurting someone or likely to, and what should be done about it. According to EPA guidance on inspections and risk assessments, the assessment identifies hazards such as deteriorated paint, lead dust and contaminated soil, then recommends how to control them.

If you are not sure which one you need, the guide on how to tell if paint is lead paint starts from what you can see in the house.

What gets checked

The assessor looks at paint condition room by room, with extra attention to friction and impact surfaces: windows, doors, stairs, railings and porch parts. Dust wipe samples are taken from floors, window sills and window troughs and sent to a lab. Soil is checked where paint has dripped or flaked, usually around the foundation and play areas. For the details on the samples themselves, see lead dust and soil testing.

Since 2024, EPA treats any reportable level of lead in dust as a hazard, which is described on the EPA hazard standards page. That is one reason a lab-backed assessment is more useful than a quick visual check.

Why Cleveland rental owners start here

Cleveland City Council passed legislation in 2019 requiring rental owners to prove that their units are lead safe. The city FAQ says an owner of a pre-1978 rental obtains a lead risk assessment and can then apply for the lead safe certificate or an exemption. The full process is covered on the page about lead safe certificates for Cleveland rentals.

Owner-occupied homes do not need the certificate, but homeowners still use assessments before buying, before remodeling or after a child's lead test.

Common questions

Who can perform a lead risk assessment in Ohio?

Ohio requires a valid lead risk assessor license for a risk assessment. The state rule sets that out, and you can ask any provider for their license number.

Does an owner-occupied home need a Cleveland lead safe certificate?

No. The city says owner-occupied properties do not need to be certified, though a risk assessment can still be a sensible step.

What happens after the report?

The report lists hazards and recommended controls. Depending on what it finds, the work may be encapsulation, window replacement or full abatement, followed by clearance testing.

Lead-Safe Window and Door Replacement for Old Cleveland Houses

Old wood windows are the classic source of lead dust in a Cleveland home: every time a painted sash rubs a painted frame, a little paint becomes powder on the sill. Replacing the sash, or the whole window, removes the lead paint on that part when the work is done with lead-safe methods.

Request a call

For service inquiries only. If someone is in immediate danger or you suspect acute poisoning, call 911 or Poison Help at 1-800-222-1222.

Why windows and doors come first

EPA lists windows and window sills, doors and door frames, stairs and porches among the most common places for lead hazards, because they take friction and impact. A painted window that sticks, rattles or gets opened daily is a steady dust source, and the dust gathers right where children play near sills and floors.

That is why many abatement plans treat windows separately from walls. If you have already had dust wipe results showing lead on the sills, windows are a natural place to start.

Replacement is not the same as demolition

Pulling out old windows with pry bars and saws can throw lead dust through the whole house. Lead-safe replacement uses containment, wet methods, HEPA vacuums and careful cleanup so the dust does not travel. Paid work that disturbs paint in a pre-1978 home falls under the EPA renovation, repair and painting rule, which requires certified firms and trained workers.

If the replacement is part of an official lead hazard fix, abatement rules apply instead. EPA explains how abatement and renovation differ, and the two kinds of certification are not interchangeable.

What replacement does and does not fix

A new window removes the lead paint on that window. It does not change the paint on the wall around it, the trim beside it or the porch outside, so the rest of the room still deserves a look. Finish with clearance testing so you know the dust is actually gone.

For houses with sound windows and other trouble spots, encapsulation or enclosure may cover the rest.

Common questions

Should I repaint my old windows instead?

Repainting a stable surface can be part of upkeep, but a window that rubs when it opens keeps making dust. An assessor can say whether repair, replacement or another method suits each window.

Does the contractor need special certification?

Yes. Paid work that disturbs paint in a pre-1978 home needs a lead-safe certified firm under the federal renovation rule, and Ohio requires licensed abatement contractors for lead hazard control work.

Will I need testing afterward?

Testing after the work is the way to confirm the dust is below the standard. See clearance testing and cleanup.
